key_features.classic_presentation: Acute appendicitis typically presents with periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) over 12-24 hours. Patients often have anorexia, nausea, and low-grade fever. Pain worsens with movement.
key_features.typical_demographics: Most common in ages 10-30 years, but can occur at any age. Slight male predominance (1.4:1). Lifetime risk approximately 7-8%.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Obstruction of appendiceal lumen leads to increased intraluminal pressure, bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, and potential perforation if untreated.

expected_positive_responses: began in center of stomach then moved right
negative_responses: pain has always been in same spot
diagnostic_questions.context: Classic migration from periumbilical to RLQ is highly specific for appendicitis. Ask specifically about whether pain started in one location and moved.

expected_positive_responses: can't jump or cough without severe pain
diagnostic_questions.context: Appendicitis pain is typically constant and severe, unlike crampy bowel obstruction or mild gastroenteritis.
Anorexia is present in >90% of appendicitis cases. Ask 'Are you hungry?' - a 'yes' makes appendicitis less likely.
Low-grade fever (100-102°F) is common. High fever (>102.5°F) may suggest perforation or alternative diagnosis.
Diarrhea can occur but profuse diarrhea suggests gastroenteritis instead.
Peritoneal irritation causes severe pain with movement. Ask if bumps in car ride hurt.
Appendicitis typically evolves over 12-48 hours. Pain >5 days suggests alternative diagnosis or perforation.

physical_exam_findings.finding: McBurney's point tenderness (RLQ, 1/3 distance from ASIS to umbilicus)
Rovsing's sign (RLQ pain with LLQ palpation)
Psoas sign (pain with right hip extension)
Obturator sign (pain with internal rotation of flexed right hip)

red_flags.symptom: Sudden severe pain that then improves briefly (may indicate perforation)
red_flags.action: Immediate surgical evaluation - possible perforation with peritonitis

red_flags.symptom: Severe pain with abdominal rigidity (board-like abdomen)
red_flags.action: Perforation with peritonitis - needs immediate surgical intervention
Possible perforation or alternative serious diagnosis (e.g., perforated diverticulitis)
Septic shock - immediate emergency care needed

distinguishing_features: Diarrhea is prominent (often more than pain)
Pain is crampy and diffuse, not localized
Often have sick contacts or recent travel
Appetite may be preserved or mildly reduced
Pain does NOT migrate from periumbilical to RLQ
Pain less severe and more diffuse
May have history of ovarian cyst
Missed period or abnormal vaginal bleeding
MUST be ruled out in all females of childbearing age
Colicky pain (comes and goes in waves)
Patient often restless (vs still with appendicitis)

diagnostic_tests.test: CT scan of abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast
diagnostic_tests.indication: Gold standard for diagnosis in adults
diagnostic_tests.typical_findings: Dilated appendix >6mm, appendiceal wall thickening, periappendiceal fat stranding, appendicolith

diagnostic_tests.indication: First-line in children and pregnant women (avoids radiation)
Rule out UTI, may show mild pyuria if appendix near bladder
diagnostic_tests.typical_findings: Usually normal or mild pyuria (<20 WBC)

diagnostic_tests.indication: ALL females of childbearing age to rule out ectopic pregnancy

treatment_summary: Appendectomy (surgical removal) is definitive treatment. Laparoscopic approach preferred. Pre-operative antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole). IV fluids, pain control, NPO. Surgery typically within 12-24 hours of diagnosis. Some uncomplicated cases may be managed with antibiotics alone, but surgery remains gold standard.

evidence_source.primary_reference: American College of Surgeons. Acute Appendicitis Clinical Practice Guidelines, 2023
